title: How Galaxies Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how galaxies work: the Milky Way's place in the universe (about a quarter of the way from the galactic center to the edge), the history of the "island universe" debate between Harlow Shapley and Hubble, Hubble's classification of galaxies as elliptical, spiral, and irregular, and the structure of the Milky Way (spiral arms, nucleus, bulge, halo, globular clusters). They cover how galaxies formed after the Big Bang, galaxy collisions and mergers (including the coming Milky Way-Andromeda merger), galaxy clusters and superclusters, the intergalactic medium, Hubble's law and red shifting, the expanding universe and the visible universe, active galaxies (Seyfert galaxies, radio galaxies, blazars, quasars) with supermassive black holes, and starburst galaxies. The episode also includes a tangent on the James Webb Space Telescope replacing Hubble, a Star Wars parsec joke, and a closing listener mail segment about stalking feedback.

segments.title: Opening banter and scale of the universe
segments.summary: The hosts joke around, then explain the scale of the solar system, Milky Way, and universe using a grain-of-sand analogy, and note that the Sun is not at the galactic center.

segments.title: History of the island universe debate
segments.summary: The Greeks named the galaxy 'galaxias' meaning milky circle. Early Western thinkers believed the visible stars were the whole universe. Harlow Shapley argued the spiral nebulae were separate galaxies outside the Milky Way, which Hubble's telescope observations later supported.

segments.title: James Webb telescope and Hubble's view back in time
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the James Webb Space Telescope as the successor to Hubble, and how telescopes see back in time because light takes time to travel, with Hubble seeing to about four million years after the Big Bang.

segments.title: Hubble's galaxy classification
segments.summary: Hubble classified galaxies as elliptical, spiral, and irregular. Ellipticals range from E0 to E7 and are disordered; spirals are bright, have arms, and rotate in order. Barred spirals have an elongated central bar, and irregular galaxies are faint and small.

segments.title: Structure of the Milky Way
segments.summary: The Milky Way is a barred spiral with a nucleus, bulge, galactic disc, four spiral arms, the Orion arm where the solar system sits, globular clusters, and a halo. The hosts discuss the galaxy's rotation period and its bent, sombrero-like shape.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: The hosts take a break before continuing.

segments.title: Galaxy formation after the Big Bang
segments.summary: Galaxies are thought to have formed about fourteen billion years ago from dust and gas clouds in the early universe, with denser regions slowing expansion and gravity pulling gas together into stars within a proto-galaxy.

segments.title: Galaxy collisions and mergers
segments.summary: Galaxies are far apart, so stars rarely collide even when galaxies merge. Examples include the Mice and the Cartwheel galaxy. Spirals often become elliptical after merging, and the Milky Way and Andromeda are expected to merge in about five billion years.

segments.title: Galaxy clusters and the local group
segments.summary: Galaxies cluster through gravity. The Milky Way belongs to the Local Group, which has about fifty galaxies, while rich clusters have more than a thousand, such as the Virgo supercluster.

segments.title: Intergalactic medium and Hubble's law
segments.summary: The intergalactic medium is the space between galaxies, containing cold and very hot gas with unexplained temperature differences. Hubble's law states that galaxies move away from us faster the farther they are, implying an expanding universe with no center and a visible universe smaller than the whole universe, with red shift as the evidence.

segments.title: Active galaxies and quasars
segments.summary: Active galaxies emit most of their light and energy from a small central nucleus, thought to be driven by supermassive black holes with jets. The four types are Seyfert galaxies, radio galaxies, quasars, and blazars, which differ mainly by viewing angle.

segments.title: Starburst galaxies
segments.summary: Starburst galaxies form stars at a rate of over a hundred per year, far above the typical one per year, and burn out quickly, possibly leaving behind globular clusters.

segments.title: Listener mail on stalking episode
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners who wrote in about their stalking episode, say they will not read the personal stories, and point to resources such as the Stalking Resource Center and the National Center for Victims of Crime.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode, invite listeners to visit the website and send email, and sign off.
